task: DP History Paper 2 essay (Topic 12: The Cold War). To what extent was ideology the main cause of the Cold War between 1945 and 1949?
text:
The breakdown of the Grand Alliance between 1945 and 1949 has been explained in three broad ways: as a clash of incompatible ideologies, as a traditional contest over security and power, and as the product of mutual misperception. This essay argues that ideology was a necessary condition for the Cold War, because it shaped how each side read the other's actions, but that it was not sufficient on its own. It was the power vacuum in Europe and the specific decisions taken over Germany and Eastern Europe that turned ideological suspicion into open confrontation.

Ideology clearly mattered. Marxism-Leninism taught Soviet leaders that conflict with capitalism was inevitable, and Stalin's election speech of February 1946 restated this publicly. American policy, in turn, rested on the belief that open markets and self-determination were the basis of peace, as set out in the Atlantic Charter of 1941. These world views made each side interpret the other in the worst light: Kennan's Long Telegram (February 1946) described Soviet policy as driven by an ideology that needed an external enemy, while Novikov's telegram later that year portrayed the USA as bent on world supremacy. Orthodox historians such as Feis, and later Gaddis in 'We Now Know' (1997), use this to argue that Stalin's ideological ambitions made the conflict unavoidable. However, ideology cannot explain the timing. The two systems had been opposed since 1917, yet they co-operated between 1941 and 1945. Something else changed in 1945.

What changed was the balance of power. The defeat of Germany left the Red Army in control of Eastern Europe, and Stalin's priority there was security more than revolution. The USSR had lost around 27 million people and had been invaded through Poland twice in thirty years, so a friendly Poland was, as he said at Yalta, a matter of 'life and death'. His behaviour was often pragmatic: he kept the percentages agreement with Churchill by giving no help to the Greek communists, and he discouraged communist seizures of power in France and Italy. This supports the revisionist view that Soviet policy was defensive and opportunistic. Nevertheless, the methods used, such as the rigged Polish election of January 1947 and the Czech coup of February 1948, looked to the West exactly like ideological expansion, which shows how security motives and ideological perception reinforced each other.

American actions were also driven by more than ideology. Revisionists such as William Appleman Williams argue that the USA needed open markets to avoid a return to depression, and the Marshall Plan of June 1947, which offered $13 billion on condition of economic openness, fits this interpretation. Stalin read it as 'dollar imperialism' and responded with Cominform and Comecon. Yet the Truman Doctrine of March 1947 was framed in explicitly ideological language, as a choice between 'two ways of life', largely in order to persuade Congress to fund aid to Greece and Turkey. Here ideology was a tool used to sell a strategic policy, which suggests it was as much a consequence of the rivalry as a cause of it.

Germany shows the interaction most clearly. Disagreement over reparations at Potsdam, the creation of Bizonia in January 1947 and the new Deutschmark in June 1948 were economic and strategic disputes, but they led directly to the Berlin Blockade, the formation of NATO in April 1949 and the division of Germany. By 1949 each step had been justified ideologically, which hardened the division.

In conclusion, ideology was the lens, not the engine. It explains why co-operation was fragile and why each defensive move was read as aggression, but the immediate causes lay in the power vacuum of 1945 and in competing security and economic interests in Europe. Ideology was therefore an essential underlying cause but not the main one; the post-revisionist emphasis on mutual misperception is the most convincing explanation overall.

task: DP History Paper 2 essay (Topic 12: The Cold War). To what extent was ideology the main cause of the Cold War between 1945 and 1949?
text:
The Cold War started after the Second World War between the USA and the USSR. Ideology was an important cause of the Cold War but there were also other causes such as the actions of the leaders and events in Europe.

The USA was capitalist and democratic, which meant people could vote and own businesses. The USSR was communist under Stalin, which meant a one-party state where the government owned industry. These two ideologies were opposite and both sides thought the other wanted to destroy them. This created mistrust. For example, in 1946 Churchill made his Iron Curtain speech saying that Europe was divided, and Kennan sent the Long Telegram saying that the USSR wanted to expand. This shows that ideology was a cause because the West saw communism as a threat.

Another cause was the conferences. At Yalta in February 1945 the Big Three agreed to divide Germany into zones and Stalin promised free elections in Eastern Europe. At Potsdam in July 1945 relations were worse because Roosevelt had died and Truman was more aggressive towards Stalin. Truman also had the atomic bomb, which he did not tell Stalin about properly. Stalin did not hold free elections and set up communist governments in countries like Poland, Hungary and Romania. This made the USA angry.

In 1947 Truman announced the Truman Doctrine, which said the USA would help countries fighting communism, and then the Marshall Plan gave money to Europe. Stalin did not let Eastern European countries take the money. In 1948 Stalin blockaded Berlin and the West had to fly in supplies for almost a year in the Berlin Airlift. After this NATO was formed in 1949.

Some historians blame Stalin and some blame the USA. I think both were responsible.

In conclusion, ideology was the main cause of the Cold War to a large extent because capitalism and communism could not exist together, but events like the Berlin Blockade also made it worse.

task: DP History internal assessment (historical investigation): To what extent was the reparations settlement imposed after the First World War responsible for the German hyperinflation of 1923?
text:
Section 1: Identification and evaluation of sources

This investigation asks: to what extent was the reparations settlement of 1921 responsible for the German hyperinflation of 1923?

Source A is John Maynard Keynes, 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace' (1919). Its origin is valuable: Keynes was the British Treasury's representative at the Paris Peace Conference, with direct access to the figures and negotiators, so his purpose, to warn that Germany could not pay what was demanded, rests on first-hand knowledge. Its content shows how the burden was understood at the time, and its influence on British and German opinion makes it part of the history itself. However, it was written in 1919, two years before the London Schedule fixed the sum and four years before the hyperinflation, so it predicts and cannot explain. Keynes had resigned in protest and wrote polemically to change policy, so he stresses German weakness and ignores German fiscal choices.

Source B is Gerald Feldman, 'The Great Disorder' (1993), by an American economic historian. Its origin gives it the value of hindsight and of Reichsbank and ministry archives unavailable to Keynes, and its purpose is academic explanation, not persuasion. Its content follows budget and currency policy month by month, allowing reparations to be weighed against domestic causes. Its limitation is that this focus on German decision-making can understate the external pressure of Allied demands, and Feldman admits that the counterfactual, what Germany would have done without reparations, cannot be tested.

Section 2: Investigation

The traditional view, following Keynes, is that reparations destroyed the mark. The London Schedule of May 1921 set the bill at 132 billion gold marks, and the mark fell from about 60 to the dollar in May to around 270 by November as the first cash payments were made. Because payment had to be in gold or foreign currency, the government sold paper marks on the exchanges, pushing their value down.

However, the inflation predates reparations. Germany financed the war mainly by borrowing and printing, not taxation, and the mark had lost most of its pre-war value by 1920, before any schedule existed. Feldman shows that post-war governments kept running deficits to pay for pensions, food subsidies and jobs because they feared revolution more than inflation. Sally Marks argues further that the real burden was far lighter than the headline figure, since the 82 billion of 'C bonds' were never expected to be paid, leaving about 50 billion, and that German leaders had an incentive to let the currency fall to prove they could not pay. On this view reparations were the excuse, not the cause.

The strongest case for reparations lies in confidence and the Ruhr. After Rathenau's murder in June 1922 foreign holders sold marks, and Feldman accepts that the unresolved reparations question removed any reason to expect stabilisation. When Germany defaulted, France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr in January 1923. The decision to fund passive resistance by printing money turned high inflation into hyperinflation: the mark went from about 18,000 to the dollar in January to 4.2 trillion in November. The occupation was a consequence of reparations, but the response was a German choice, and the speed with which the Rentenmark stabilised prices in November 1923, while reparations were still owed, shows that monetary policy was decisive.

Reparations were therefore responsible only to a limited extent. They did not create the inflation and their real weight was exaggerated, but they damaged confidence and provoked the Ruhr crisis that triggered the final collapse. The underlying cause was German fiscal and monetary policy from 1914 onwards.

Section 3: Reflection

This investigation showed me a challenge historians face: sources on economic causes carry political purposes. Keynes's figures looked objective until I compared them with Marks, and I realised that choosing which number to quote, 132 billion or 50 billion, is already an interpretation. I also found that comparing chronology with exchange-rate data cannot prove causation, because confidence cannot be measured directly and must be inferred from behaviour. Unlike a scientist, I could not test the counterfactual of 'no reparations', which is why Feldman and Marks reach different conclusions from similar evidence.

task: DP History internal assessment (historical investigation): To what extent was the reparations settlement imposed after the First World War responsible for the German hyperinflation of 1923?
text:
Section 1: Evaluation of sources

My research question is: To what extent was the Treaty of Versailles responsible for the hyperinflation in Germany in 1923?

The first source is 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace' by John Maynard Keynes, written in 1919. Keynes was a British economist who was at the peace conference. The source is valuable because he was there at the time so he is a primary source and knew what was happening. It is limited because he could be biased as he did not agree with the treaty.

The second source is a textbook, 'Weimar and Nazi Germany' by John Hite and Chris Hinton (2000). It is valuable because it was written by historians with hindsight and has many facts. It is limited because it is a school textbook so it does not go into much detail.

Section 2: Investigation

The Treaty of Versailles was signed in June 1919. Germany had to accept the war guilt clause, Article 231, and pay reparations. In 1921 the amount was fixed at £6.6 billion. This shows the treaty was a cause because Germany did not have the money.

In 1922 Germany failed to pay, so in January 1923 French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr. The German government told the workers to go on strike, which was called passive resistance, and paid them by printing more money. This caused hyperinflation. By November 1923 a loaf of bread cost 200 billion marks and people carried their wages in wheelbarrows.

However there were other causes. Germany had already printed money during the war to pay for it, so inflation had already started before the treaty. Keynes said the reparations were too high, but some historians say Germany could have paid.

In conclusion, the Treaty of Versailles was responsible to a large extent, because without reparations the Ruhr would not have been occupied.

Section 3: Reflection

During this investigation I learned that historians have different views and that sources can be biased. I learned to use both primary and secondary sources to get a balanced view.

task: DP Economics IA commentary (Microeconomics) on a news article reporting that Scotland raised its minimum unit price for alcohol from 50p to 65p.
text:
Commentary 1
Article: 'Minimum unit price for alcohol rises to 65p in Scotland', BBC News, 30 September 2024
Unit: Microeconomics
Key concept: Intervention
Word count: 792

The article reports that the Scottish Government has raised its minimum unit price (MUP) for alcohol from 50p to 65p, arguing that inflation had eroded the original floor and that alcohol-specific deaths are at their highest since 2008. An MUP is a price floor: a legal minimum price set above the market equilibrium. The government is intervening because alcohol is a demerit good whose consumption creates negative externalities, costs to third parties that are not reflected in the market price.

Figure 1: Negative consumption externality in the alcohol market. Price, costs and benefits on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis. MPB lies above MSB; supply is S = MPC = MSC. Market equilibrium is at Qm, Pm where MPB = MPC; the social optimum is at Qopt where MSB = MSC. The triangle between Qopt and Qm is shaded as welfare loss.

As Figure 1 shows, drinkers consider only their marginal private benefit, so the market quantity Qm exceeds the socially optimal Qopt. For every unit between Qopt and Qm, marginal social cost is greater than marginal social benefit because of external costs such as the NHS treatment and policing mentioned in the article. This overconsumption is a market failure, and the shaded area is the welfare loss.

Figure 2: Price floor on cheap alcohol. D and S intersect at Pe (50p) and Qe. A horizontal line at Pmin (65p) lies above equilibrium; quantity demanded falls to Qd, quantity supplied rises to Qs, and the surplus Qs - Qd is labelled.

In Figure 2 the floor is binding for the cheapest products, such as strong cider. Quantity demanded contracts from Qe to Qd, moving consumption towards Qopt and reducing the welfare loss in Figure 1. Unlike an indirect tax, the higher price is not collected by the government: it is kept by retailers, so consumer surplus is transferred to producers instead of funding treatment services, which is why charities quoted in the article call for a levy on retailers.

How far the intervention works depends on price elasticity of demand. Moderate drinkers have substitutes, so their demand for cheap alcohol is relatively elastic. However, the dependent drinkers the policy most needs to reach have price-inelastic demand because of addiction: the percentage fall in quantity is smaller than the percentage rise in price, so their spending rises. The article quotes a homelessness charity warning that some are cutting back on food instead. The policy is therefore regressive, since the increase takes a larger share of income from low-income households, while wealthier consumers buying alcohol already priced above 65p per unit are unaffected. This is a cost in terms of equity.

On the other hand, the article cites Public Health Scotland's estimate that the original 50p floor reduced alcohol-specific deaths by 13 percent, which suggests that in practice heavy drinkers of the cheapest alcohol did respond. The floor targets exactly the products linked to the most harm, which a general excise tax cannot do. In the long run demand is also likely to become more elastic as habits change and fewer young people begin drinking heavily. A risk is that consumers switch to buying across the border in England, which would weaken the effect and not appear in Scottish sales data.

Overall, raising the floor to 65p is a justified intervention to correct a market failure, and restoring its real value is logical because inflation had made it less binding. However, because it works only through price it is most effective for hazardous drinkers and least effective for dependent ones. It would be both more effective and more equitable if combined with spending on treatment, ideally funded by a levy on the extra retailer revenue that the price floor creates.

task: DP Economics IA commentary (Microeconomics) on a news article reporting that Scotland raised its minimum unit price for alcohol from 50p to 65p.
text:
Article: 'Minimum unit price for alcohol rises to 65p in Scotland', BBC News
Key concept: Intervention

The article is about the Scottish government increasing the minimum price of alcohol from 50p to 65p per unit. The government is doing this because too many people are dying from alcohol and it costs the NHS a lot of money. This is an example of government intervention in a market.

A minimum price is a price floor. This is when the government sets a price that firms are not allowed to sell below. Alcohol is a demerit good, which means it is bad for you and people consume too much of it. It also has negative externalities, which are bad effects on other people, for example drunk people causing crime.

Figure 1: Price floor diagram. Demand and supply curves cross at P1 and Q1. A line is drawn above this at 65p. Quantity demanded is Q2 and quantity supplied is Q3.

As the diagram shows, when the price goes up to 65p the demand for alcohol goes down from Q1 to Q2. This means people drink less alcohol, which is what the government wants. There is also excess supply because firms want to sell more at the higher price.

This will have effects on different people. Consumers will have to pay more for alcohol, especially cheap alcohol like cider. Producers and shops will get more money for each drink they sell but they will sell fewer drinks. The government will spend less on healthcare because there will be fewer people in hospital.

However, the policy might not work because alcohol is addictive so demand is inelastic. This means that even when the price goes up people will still buy it. Also people might go to England to buy cheaper alcohol.

In conclusion, I think the minimum price is a good policy because it will reduce drinking and save lives, although it might not work for everyone. The government has intervened in the market to make it better for society.

task: DP Geography IA fieldwork report (Option A: Freshwater). To what extent do the channel characteristics of the River Holford, Somerset, change downstream as predicted by the Bradshaw model?
text:
Fieldwork question: To what extent do the channel characteristics of the River Holford, Somerset, change downstream as predicted by the Bradshaw model?

1. Fieldwork question and geographic context
This investigation links to Option A, Freshwater (drainage basin hydrology and geomorphology). The Bradshaw model predicts that width, depth, velocity and discharge increase downstream while bedload size decreases. The Holford is a 7 km stream draining the Quantock Hills to the Bristol Channel at Kilve. It is suitable because it can be sampled from source to mouth in one day and crosses a geological boundary from resistant Devonian sandstone to softer Jurassic shale. Figure 1: annotated 1:25,000 map of the catchment showing the eight sites, the geology boundary and the tributary confluence. Hypotheses: H1 width and depth increase downstream; H2 velocity increases downstream; H3 bedload size decreases downstream.

2. Methods of investigation
Data were collected on 14 May 2025 at base flow. Eight sites were chosen by systematic sampling at roughly 800 m intervals, adjusted to the nearest safe access point. Width was measured with a tape held taut at right angles to the flow. Depth was measured with a metre rule at five equally spaced points to give a mean and a cross-sectional area. Velocity was measured with a flow meter at 0.6 of the depth at three points across the channel, because surface floats overestimate mean velocity. Fifteen stones per site were chosen by systematic point sampling across the bed, to avoid bias towards large, visible stones, and the long axis measured with callipers.

3. Quality and treatment of information
Figure 2: cross-sections of all eight sites drawn to one scale. Figure 3: scatter graphs with best-fit lines for width, velocity and bedload against distance. Figure 4: proportional bars for discharge located on the base map. Spearman's rank was used because it suits a small sample and does not assume a normal distribution. Width against distance gave rs = 0.93 and bedload against distance rs = -0.88, both beyond the critical value of 0.738 (n = 8, 0.05 level). Velocity gave rs = 0.52, below the critical value.

4. Written analysis
Width increased from 0.9 m at site 1 to 4.6 m at site 8 and mean depth from 0.06 m to 0.31 m, so H1 is accepted. The increase is not steady: Figure 3 shows a step between sites 4 and 5, where width rises from 2.1 m to 3.4 m. Figure 1 explains this, since the Hodder's Combe tributary joins here and discharge rises from 0.05 to 0.19 cumecs. Mean bedload fell from 11.2 cm to 3.9 cm and stones became visibly rounder, consistent with attrition, so H3 is accepted. The sharpest fall comes after site 5, where the channel crosses onto shale, which breaks down faster, so geology as well as distance explains the pattern.

Velocity is the anomaly. It rose overall from 0.21 to 0.48 m/s, but site 6 recorded only 0.19 m/s. Figure 2 shows that site 6, just upstream of a weir, is wide and shallow, with a hydraulic radius of 0.09 m compared with 0.17 m at site 5, so more energy is lost to friction. H2 is only partly supported: the trend exists but is not statistically significant, and human modification of the channel disrupts the model.

5. Conclusion
The Holford conforms to the Bradshaw model to a large extent for width, depth, discharge and bedload, with significant correlations, but only partly for velocity. A tributary, a geological boundary and a weir explain the departures from the model.

6. Evaluation
The main weakness is that data come from a single day at low flow and may not represent winter conditions. Fifteen stones is a small sample, and the long axis ignores shape; Power's roundness index would test attrition directly. Eight sites is close to the minimum for Spearman's rank, and extra sites between 5 and 7 would show whether site 6 is a true anomaly. The question could be modified to compare the Holford with a nearby unmodified stream to isolate the effect of the weir.

Word count: 2,470. Figures are numbered and referred to in the text; sources are in the bibliography.

task: DP Geography IA fieldwork report (Option A: Freshwater). To what extent do the channel characteristics of the River Holford, Somerset, change downstream as predicted by the Bradshaw model?
text:
Fieldwork question: How does the River Holford change downstream?

Introduction
The River Holford is a river in Somerset. It starts in the Quantock Hills and flows to the sea at Kilve. The Bradshaw model says that rivers get wider, deeper and faster as they go downstream and the rocks get smaller. I want to see if this is true for the River Holford. Figure 1 is a map of the river from Google Maps. My hypothesis is that the river will get wider and faster downstream.

Method
We visited 5 sites along the river. At each site we measured the width with a tape measure and the depth with a ruler in three places. For velocity we timed how long a cork took to float 5 metres and did this three times. We also picked up 10 rocks at each site and measured them.

Results
Figure 2 is a bar chart of the width at each site. Figure 3 is a bar chart of velocity. Figure 4 is a bar chart of rock size.

Analysis
Figure 2 shows that the width increased from 1.1 m at site 1 to 4.2 m at site 5. This agrees with the Bradshaw model. The depth also increased from 7 cm to 28 cm. This is because more water joins the river from tributaries as it goes downstream. Figure 3 shows the velocity went up from 0.2 m/s at site 1 to 0.4 m/s at site 5, but at site 4 it was slower, 0.15 m/s. This was an anomaly. Figure 4 shows the rocks got smaller, from 10 cm to 4 cm, because of erosion.

Conclusion
My hypothesis was correct. The river got wider, deeper and faster downstream so the River Holford fits the Bradshaw model.

Evaluation
One problem was that the cork sometimes got stuck on rocks so we had to start again. Also it was hard to measure the width where there were plants on the bank. If I did it again I would visit more sites and go on a different day.

task: DP Business Management IA (research project, key concept: change). To what extent will extending evening opening be an effective growth strategy for Greggs plc?
text:
Research question: To what extent will extending evening opening be an effective growth strategy for Greggs plc?
Key concept: Change

Introduction
Greggs plc is the UK's largest bakery chain, with 2,473 shops and sales of £1.81 billion in 2023 (Greggs Annual Report 2023). Its traditional strength is breakfast and lunch, but management describes the evening, after 4 pm, as its fastest-growing daypart, and has extended hours and added hot food such as pizza in over 1,200 shops. This is a significant change in what the business is, from a bakery towards a food-on-the-go rival of McDonald's and KFC. The question matters because the lunchtime market is close to saturation, so future growth depends on whether this change succeeds. Five supporting documents are used: the 2023 annual report, a 2024 trading update, a Mintel report on eating out, and articles from the Financial Times and The Grocer, chosen to give views from outside the company. The tools applied are the Ansoff matrix, SWOT analysis and profit margin.

Analysis
In Ansoff's terms, evening trading combines product development, new menu items for existing customers, with market penetration through longer hours in existing shops. This is lower risk than diversification because Greggs keeps its core competence of low-cost centralised production and uses assets it already pays for. Rent is a fixed cost, so each extra evening sale spreads it over more units. The annual report shows evening sales reached about 9 percent of company-managed shop sales and like-for-like sales grew 13.7 percent, which suggests the strategy is contributing to growth.

However, the profitability data are less clear. Underlying pre-tax profit was £167.7 million on sales of £1,810 million, a margin of 9.3 percent, down from 9.8 percent in 2022 despite the sales growth. Evening trading adds variable costs, particularly labour, at a time when the National Living Wage rose by nearly 10 percent. The Grocer points out that hot evening products earn lower margins than a sausage roll because they need more preparation and create more waste. So revenue growth has not become margin growth, and the published accounts do not separate the evening contribution from new shop openings, which is a limitation of secondary data.

The SWOT analysis shows the strategic tension. The key strength is value: Mintel reports that price is the main reason consumers choose Greggs, an advantage in a cost-of-living squeeze. The weakness is perception and format: consumers associate Greggs with daytime snacks, and many shops are small, with little seating, on high streets where evening footfall is low. The opportunity is delivery through Just Eat and Uber Eats, already 5.6 percent of sales, which removes the seating problem. The threat is that competitors have drive-throughs, larger evening menus and decades of customer habit; the FT quotes an analyst who doubts a bakery can become a 'dinner destination'.

Evaluation
The evening strategy is effective as a way of using existing capacity: the extra investment is small, the risk is low and the sales evidence is positive. It is less convincing as the main engine of long-term growth, because the evidence that it raises profit and not just revenue is weak, and its success depends on changing consumer habits, which is slow and outside Greggs's control. The sources must also be weighed: the annual report is written for shareholders and is likely to be optimistic, the analyst's view is opinion, and the Mintel survey, though the most neutral, measures intentions, not purchases.

Conclusion
Extending evening opening will be effective to a moderate extent. It is a sensible, low-risk change that raises revenue from existing assets, but on the available evidence it is not improving margins and is unlikely by itself to deliver the growth Greggs has promised. I recommend concentrating evening hours on locations with proven evening footfall, such as retail parks and transport hubs, and on delivery, instead of extending hours everywhere. A firmer judgment would need shop-level profit data, which are not public.

Bibliography: five supporting documents and course textbook, referenced in full. Word count: 1,795.

task: DP Business Management IA (research project, key concept: change). To what extent will extending evening opening be an effective growth strategy for Greggs plc?
text:
Research question: Should Greggs open in the evening?

Introduction
Greggs is a bakery chain in the UK which sells sausage rolls, sandwiches, pasties and coffee. It was founded in 1939 in Newcastle and now has more than 2,000 shops. It is a public limited company. Recently Greggs has started opening later in the evening and selling new products like pizza. I chose this topic because I go to Greggs often and I noticed the shop near me is open later. I will use a SWOT analysis and the Ansoff matrix to answer my question.

SWOT analysis
Strengths: Greggs has a strong brand and low prices. It has many shops and loyal customers. The vegan sausage roll was very successful.
Weaknesses: The food is seen as unhealthy. Most shops are small and do not have seats.
Opportunities: Opening in the evening. Delivery with Just Eat. More people want cheap food because of the cost of living.
Threats: Competitors such as McDonald's, KFC and Subway. Rising costs of ingredients and wages.

The SWOT shows that Greggs has more strengths than weaknesses so it is in a good position to open in the evening.

Ansoff matrix
The Ansoff matrix has four strategies: market penetration, market development, product development and diversification. Opening in the evening is market development because Greggs is selling to a new market of evening customers. This is medium risk.

Finance
Greggs made sales of £1.8 billion in 2023, which was higher than 2022. This shows the business is growing and can afford to open in the evening. However, opening in the evening will increase costs because staff need to be paid for more hours.

Conclusion
In conclusion Greggs should open in the evening because it has a strong brand and its sales are increasing. There are some threats from competitors but Greggs is cheaper. Opening in the evening will increase revenue and profit.

Sources: Greggs website, BBC News, Wikipedia.

task: DP Business Management IA (research project, key concept: change). To what extent will extending evening opening be an effective growth strategy for Greggs plc?
text:

A SWOT is strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. A strength of Greggs is the sausage rolls. A weakness is that it is unhealthy.

In conclusion Greggs is doing well and should carry on opening in the evening and it will make more profit.

task: DP Extended Essay, English A: Literature (Category 1). How does Kazuo Ishiguro use Stevens's unreliable narration to present self-deception in 'The Remains of the Day'?
text:
Research question: How does Kazuo Ishiguro use Stevens's unreliable narration to present self-deception in 'The Remains of the Day' (1989)?

Introduction
Stevens, an English butler, narrates a motoring trip in 1956 while recalling his service to Lord Darlington in the 1930s. Critics agree that he is unreliable, but Wall (1994) notes that the novel challenges the usual definition, because Stevens rarely lies about events. This essay asks how the unreliability works at the level of language. It argues that Ishiguro locates self-deception not in what Stevens reports but in three habits of narration: displacing feeling into professional vocabulary, revising memory, and shifting from 'I' to 'one'. The method is close reading of four episodes, supported by narratological criticism (Booth, Phelan, Wall).

Professional language as evasion
Stevens defines 'dignity' as a butler's ability not to abandon 'the professional being he inhabits'. The verb 'inhabits' makes the role a building he lives inside, and Ishiguro shows it working as shelter. On the night his father dies during the 1923 conference, Stevens goes on serving, and his grief reaches us only through another character: Lord Darlington says, 'You look as though you're crying.' Stevens neither confirms nor denies it, and later calls the evening a 'triumph'. The reader perceives in that gap what the narrator will not say. Phelan calls this underreporting; I would add that it is also misreading, since Stevens appears to have persuaded himself that what he felt was professional pride.

The revision of memory
Ishiguro makes Stevens correct himself. He attributes a remark about his father's errors to Miss Kenton, then decides it was Lord Darlington. He remembers standing outside Miss Kenton's door, sure she was crying, then moves the memory to a different evening. These slips could be read as the realism of an ageing memory. However, they cluster around moments of guilt, and each revision moves responsibility or emotion away from Stevens. The reader learns to distrust him most when he is most insistent, as when he claims his 'every instinct opposed' dismissing the two Jewish maids, although at the time he said nothing and rebuked Miss Kenton for objecting.

The pronoun 'one'
The most consistent marker is grammatical. When emotion threatens, Stevens abandons 'I': 'One could presumably drive oneself to distraction in this way.' The impersonal pronoun turns a private regret into a general rule about people, not a fact about him. Its absence is therefore significant. When Miss Kenton admits at Weymouth that she has imagined a life with him, he says, 'at that moment, my heart was breaking.' It is the only time he names an emotion in the first person without qualification, and its plainness after two hundred pages of evasion gives it force. It also complicates the label 'unreliable': Stevens can tell the truth, which suggests the earlier evasions were in some buried sense chosen.

Counter-argument
It could be objected that calling Stevens self-deceived underestimates his awareness, since a man who knew nothing could not hide it so skilfully. The ending partly supports this: on the pier he admits he cannot even say he made his own mistakes. Yet he immediately resolves to practise 'bantering' for his new employer, turning insight back into duty. Ishiguro therefore presents self-deception as a process never complete in either direction.

Conclusion
Ishiguro presents self-deception through the texture of narration: professional euphemism, self-revising memory and the retreat into 'one'. The reader is positioned to see what Stevens cannot say, and the one unguarded sentence at Weymouth shows how much the technique has withheld.

Bibliography: primary text and six critical sources in MLA format.

Reflections on planning and progress
First reflection: I wanted to write about 'regret', but my supervisor pointed out this was a theme, not a question. Interim reflection: my draft summarised too much plot. I colour-coded every use of 'one' in three chapters and found the pattern broke at Weymouth, which changed my argument; I had not expected the evidence to contradict my plan. Final reflection: the viva voce made me realise I had quoted critics as authorities instead of testing them. If I began again I would choose the episodes after the close reading, not before.

task: DP Extended Essay, English A: Literature (Category 1). How does Kazuo Ishiguro use Stevens's unreliable narration to present self-deception in 'The Remains of the Day'?
text:
Research question: How is Stevens presented in The Remains of the Day?

Introduction
The Remains of the Day is a novel by Kazuo Ishiguro published in 1989. I chose this novel because I enjoyed it in class and I find the character of Stevens interesting. In this essay I will look at how Stevens is presented as a butler, his relationship with Miss Kenton and his relationship with Lord Darlington.

Stevens as a butler
Stevens is presented as a very dedicated butler. He talks a lot about 'dignity' and what makes a great butler. For example, when his father dies during an important conference he carries on working. This shows that he puts his job before his family. Ishiguro uses formal language for Stevens to show that he is always professional, even when he is talking to the reader.

Stevens and Miss Kenton
It is clear to the reader that she has feelings for Stevens, for example when she brings flowers to his room. However, Stevens does not show his feelings. He is an unreliable narrator because he does not tell us what he really feels. At the end he says his 'heart was breaking', which shows that he did love her.

Stevens and Lord Darlington
Lord Darlington was a Nazi sympathiser. When Lord Darlington tells him to fire two Jewish maids, he does it. Later he denies having worked for Lord Darlington. This shows he is ashamed.

Conclusion
In conclusion, Stevens is presented as a loyal and professional butler who has wasted his life. Ishiguro uses first person narration and formal language to present him. The novel shows that people should not put work before love.

Bibliography: The Remains of the Day; SparkNotes; one online review.

Reflections on planning and progress
First: I chose my book and my supervisor told me to narrow down my question. Interim: I have written 2,000 words and need to add more quotes. Final: I finished my essay. I found it hard to reach the word count but I managed my time well.

task: DP Theory of Knowledge essay. Is replicability necessary in the production of knowledge? Discuss with reference to the natural sciences and history.
text:
Replicability means that a knowledge claim can be reached again by someone else following the same method. The title asks whether this is 'necessary', that is, whether without it no knowledge is produced. I will argue that replicability of results is necessary only for one kind of knowledge, general claims about how things regularly behave, but that a broader requirement, that others can re-examine the route to a claim, is necessary in both the natural sciences and history.

In the natural sciences replicability appears to be the test that separates knowledge from error. In 1989 Fleischmann and Pons announced 'cold fusion' in a tabletop cell; within months other laboratories failed to reproduce the excess heat and the claim was rejected. In 2011 the OPERA experiment measured neutrinos apparently travelling faster than light; the team asked others to check, and the result was traced to a loose fibre-optic cable. In both cases the community refused to accept a result on one team's authority. This fits the aim of science to produce general laws. If a claim says that under conditions C effect E always follows, then failing to obtain E under C counts directly against it. Here replicability is part of what the claim means.

However, the natural sciences also include knowledge of events that cannot be repeated. Supernova 1987A happened once. The first detection of gravitational waves in 2015 was a single event lasting a fraction of a second. What made it credible was not repetition of the event but that two detectors 3,000 km apart recorded the same signal and that the data were released for other teams to re-analyse. This suggests that what is necessary is not replication of the phenomenon but independent checkability of evidence and reasoning. A sceptic could reply that the result only became secure when later detections confirmed the pattern, so replication still does the final work. I think this is partly right, but it shows that replicability raises the degree of certainty; it does not mark a line between knowledge and non-knowledge. The replication crisis in psychology points the same way: when fewer than half of 100 published studies replicated (Open Science Collaboration, 2015), we could say either that they were never knowledge, or that they were the best-justified beliefs available and that replication is how a community corrects itself. Which we choose depends on whether knowledge is seen as a finished product or a provisional stage.

History seems at first to refute the title, because its objects are unique: the fall of the Berlin Wall cannot be re-run with one variable changed. Yet historians do not treat all accounts as equally good. In the Irving v Lipstadt trial in 2000, the historian Richard Evans went back through David Irving's footnotes to the original documents and showed that Irving had mistranslated and misdated sources to minimise Hitler's responsibility. What Evans replicated was not the past but the path from archive to claim; another historian following the same sources could not honestly arrive at Irving's conclusions. This is the same principle that made the gravitational wave result credible.

There is a real difference, though. Two honest historians can examine the same archive and disagree, for instance over whether the First World War originated mainly in German aims, as Fischer argued, or in a shared failure, as Clark argues. This is not a failure of replication. Historical knowledge includes interpretation and judgments of significance, which depend on the questions the historian brings. Demanding replicable conclusions would exclude exactly the perspective-dependent understanding the discipline values. In history the evidence must be re-traceable, but the interpretation need not be reproducible.

In conclusion, replicability in the strict sense, getting the same result again, is necessary for law-like claims in the natural sciences, but not for all scientific knowledge and not for historical interpretation. What is necessary in both areas is that the process is open to being retraced by others. The implication is that we should be wary of claims whose route cannot be inspected, however confident the source, and equally wary of dismissing knowledge of unique events simply because they happen once.

task: DP Theory of Knowledge essay. Is replicability necessary in the production of knowledge? Discuss with reference to the natural sciences and history.
text:
Replicability is when an experiment can be repeated and get the same results. In this essay I will discuss whether replicability is necessary in the natural sciences and history. I think it is necessary in science but not in history.

In the natural sciences, replicability is very important. The scientific method involves making a hypothesis, doing an experiment and then repeating it. For example, in my chemistry IA I did a titration five times to make sure my results were reliable. If I had only done it once I could not be sure that my result was correct, because there could be random errors. Also, when scientists publish a paper other scientists try to repeat the experiment through peer review. A famous example is Andrew Wakefield, who claimed that the MMR vaccine caused autism. Other scientists could not replicate his results and his paper was withdrawn. This shows that replicability is necessary in science to make sure knowledge is true.

However, some things in science cannot be replicated. For example the Big Bang only happened once and we cannot repeat it, but scientists still have knowledge about it from evidence. So replicability is not always necessary.

In history, events cannot be replicated because they happened in the past. For example we cannot repeat the Second World War to see what caused it. Historians use sources instead of experiments. Sources can be biased, so historians have to compare different sources to find out what happened. Different historians also have different perspectives, for example about who started the Cold War. This shows that history is more subjective than science and that replicability is not necessary in history, because historians still produce knowledge without it.

On the other hand, it could be said that history is less reliable than science because it cannot be replicated.

In conclusion, replicability is necessary in the natural sciences to a large extent because it makes knowledge reliable, but it is not necessary in history because history uses different methods. Therefore it depends on the area of knowledge.

task: DP Theory of Knowledge essay. Is replicability necessary in the production of knowledge? Discuss with reference to the natural sciences and history.
text:
Replicability means to copy something. In this essay I will talk about if we need replicability for knowledge.

In science you need to do experiments. Scientists do experiments in labs and they find out new knowledge like medicines and vaccines. Science is based on facts so it is always true and it can be proved. If you repeat something many times you will remember it better, which is how we learn knowledge at school, for example times tables.

History is about the past. We cannot go back to the past so we do not really know what happened and it is just opinions. History repeats itself, like how there were two world wars.

So replicability is necessary for knowledge because without it we would not know anything.
